name: Holiness movement within Methodism
description: The Holiness movement emerged chiefly within 19th-century Methodism.
narrative: The Holiness movement emerged chiefly within 19th-century Methodism. Nineteenth-century Holiness advocates revived Wesley’s teaching about love of God and neighbor and emphasized an identifiable experience of sanctifying grace. Meetings, publications, and later denominations carried this teaching beyond Methodist institutions. Some adherents remained Methodist; others formed independent Holiness churches. A portion of this environment later fed Pentecostal revival, although Holiness teaching and speaking-in-tongues Pentecostalism are not equivalent.

name: Restorationist revival
description: The Restoration Movement emerged on the American frontier during the Second Great Awakening.
narrative: The Restoration Movement emerged on the American frontier during the Second Great Awakening. Stone’s Kentucky revival circle and the Campbell movement in Pennsylvania developed separately in reaction to denominational tests of fellowship. Their streams united in 1832, but disputes about missions, worship, and church organization later divided their descendants. The 1804 date marks the dissolution of Springfield Presbytery, one formative act rather than a single founding of every Restoration church.

name: Wesleyan-Holiness denomination
description: The Church of the Nazarene emerged from the Wesleyan-Holiness movement within Methodism.
narrative: The Church of the Nazarene emerged from the Wesleyan-Holiness movement within Methodism. Regional Holiness churches united in stages, with the 1908 Pilot Point union becoming the denomination’s anniversary milestone. Its ancestry includes the Methodist teaching of sanctification and independent Holiness institutions. Subsequent mission work made it an international denomination. Its use of the language of Spirit baptism refers to sanctifying grace and must not be equated automatically with Pentecostal teaching about tongues.

name: Union in Lexington
description: Restoration Movement union in 1832 is a milestone in the Disciples lineage.
narrative: Restoration Movement union in 1832 is a milestone in the Disciples lineage. The Disciples trace their story through the 1832 union of Stone and Campbell followers. Separation from a cappella Churches of Christ developed gradually and was recognized in the 1906 census; independent Christian churches later withdrew from cooperative institutions. The present denominational structure was established through the 1968 Design. Its 1832 start therefore identifies heritage rather than the date of the modern constitution.

name: Separate census recognition after gradual division
description: The 1906 federal religious census listed Churches of Christ separately after a gradual division over worship and organized missionary activity; it was not a single founding-day separation.
narrative: The 1906 federal religious census listed Churches of Christ separately after a gradual division over worship and organized missionary activity; it was not a single founding-day separation. Congregations that opposed instrumental worship and missionary societies increasingly separated from other Restoration churches during the nineteenth century. A separate listing in the 1906 census recognized a division that had developed over time; it did not create all these churches on a single day. Without a central denominational authority, local congregations and networks developed significant internal differences.

name: Independent Christian Churches separation
description: Independent Christian Churches separated from the Disciples between 1926 and 1971.
narrative: Independent Christian Churches separated from the Disciples between 1926 and 1971. Disagreement over missionary practice and theological direction contributed to separation beginning in the 1920s. Large numbers of congregations withdrew around the Disciples restructuring of the late 1960s. Their cooperation developed through voluntary conventions and independent ministries rather than a single denomination. The 1926 date represents the beginning of a process, not a universal founding assembly.
